crops.name: Radish
crops.notes: Fastest crop in the garden — great for kids and gap-filling.

crops.name: Turnip
crops.notes: Greens are edible too.

crops.name: Carrot
crops.notes: Keep seedbed moist until germination (1–3 weeks). Loose, stone-free soil.

crops.name: Parsnip
crops.notes: Use fresh seed each year. Sweeter after frost.

crops.name: Celery
crops.notes: Heavy feeder that needs constant moisture.

crops.name: Peas
crops.notes: Fixes nitrogen — a great crop before heavy feeders. Provide a trellis.

support.tip: Peas climb with little tendrils. Put up netting or a trellis soon after they sprout so they can grab on while they are still small.

crops.name: Bush bean
crops.notes: Sow successions every 3 weeks for a steady supply.

support.tip: Pole beans climb high and keep making beans for a long time. Put a tall, strong support in place when you plant, so the vines have something to climb right away.

crops.name: Cucumber
crops.notes: Trellising saves space and keeps fruit clean.

support.tip: A trellis keeps cucumber fruit clean and saves space. Train the vines gently onto the support as they grow. Bush types can stay on the ground.

crops.name: Zucchini / summer squash
crops.notes: One or two plants feed a family. Pick small and often.

support.tip: Most zucchini plants stay low and bushy. Let them sprawl, or slip a short cage around the plant if it starts to flop.

crops.name: Winter squash
crops.notes: Cure in a warm spot 1–2 weeks after harvest for storage.

src.t: Texas A&M AgriLife (Lubbock Master Gardeners) — Vegetable Planting Calendar, recommended varieties (Hound research)

support.tip: Most winter squash needs a lot of ground. Let the vines sprawl, or grow smaller types on a very strong trellis. Sling heavy fruit so the vine does not tear.

crops.name: Pumpkin
crops.notes: Needs lots of room and a long season.

src.t: Texas A&M AgriLife (Lubbock Master Gardeners) — Vegetable Planting Calendar, recommended varieties (Hound research)

support.tip: Big pumpkins are best left to sprawl on the ground. Only small types belong on a very strong trellis, with a sling under each fruit.

crops.name: Watermelon
crops.notes: Pick "icebox" varieties for shorter seasons.

src.t: Texas A&M AgriLife (Lubbock Master Gardeners) — Vegetable Planting Calendar, recommended varieties (Hound research)

support.tip: Leave big watermelons on the ground. Small types can climb a strong trellis if you sling each melon so it does not tear the vine.

crops.name: Cantaloupe / melon
crops.notes: Ripe when the fruit slips easily off the vine.

src.t: Texas A&M AgriLife (Lubbock Master Gardeners) — Vegetable Planting Calendar, recommended varieties (Hound research)

support.tip: Melons can sprawl on the ground or climb a strong trellis. If you grow them up, sling each fruit so the vine does not break.

crops.name: Sweet corn
crops.notes: Plant in blocks of at least 4 short rows (not one long row) for good pollination. Pick when silks are brown and kernels squirt milky juice. Isolate corn types: keep field corn, popcorn, Indian corn and sweet corn ~250–300 ft apart, or plant them so tasseling is at least 14 days apart, so pollen from one does not spoil another.

crops.name: Onion
crops.notes: Choose long-day types in the north (zones 1–6), short-day in the south (7–10). Pick by day length: short-day onions for the South (below ~35°N), intermediate-day for the middle (e.g. southern Illinois), long-day for the North.

crops.name: Garlic
crops.notes: Plant cloves ~2–4 weeks before the ground freezes; harvest next summer when lower leaves brown.

crops.name: Leek
crops.notes: Hill soil up the stems for long white shanks.

src.t: Texas A&M AgriLife (Lubbock Master Gardeners) — Vegetable Planting Calendar, recommended varieties (Hound research)

crops.name: Okra
crops.notes: Thrives in heat; pick pods at 3–4 in every day or two.

crops.name: Sweet potato
crops.notes: Plant slips once soil is warm; cure roots before storing.

support.tip: The roots grow in the ground. The vines can sprawl, or you can train them up a trellis to save space. Do not lift or move the roots when you train the vines.

crops.name: Asparagus
crops.notes: Perennial — light harvest in year 2, full harvest from year 3 for 15+ years.

crops.name: Rhubarb
crops.notes: Needs winter chill. Eat stalks only — leaves are toxic.

crops.name: Strawberry
crops.notes: Day-neutral types fruit the first year; June-bearers the next.

crops.name: Raspberry
crops.notes: Fall-bearing (primocane) types are easiest to prune.

support.tip: Raspberry canes get tall and floppy. A simple trellis, or a line of stakes and wire, keeps fruit off the ground and makes picking easier.

crops.name: Blueberry
crops.notes: Needs acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5). Plant two varieties for better yields.

crops.name: Fig
crops.notes: In zone 6 and colder grow in a container and overwinter indoors.
crops.pollination: Common figs make fruit without pollination — one plant is enough.
crops.care: In zone 6 and colder, grow in a big pot and move it to a cool, frost-free place for winter.

src.t: Clemson HGIC 1354 — Fig

crops.name: Lemon (Meyer & other)
crops.notes: Frost-tender. The Meyer lemon is the most cold-tolerant lemon and grows well in a container — elsewhere grow dwarf varieties in pots and bring them in before frost.

src.t: UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions — Citrus (Hound research)

crops.name: Basil
crops.notes: Pinch flower buds to keep leaves coming. Hates cold nights.

crops.name: Parsley
crops.notes: Slow to germinate — soak seed overnight. Host plant for swallowtail caterpillars.

crops.name: Cilantro
crops.notes: Bolts quickly in heat; seeds are coriander.

crops.name: Dill
crops.notes: Attracts beneficial insects; self-seeds readily.

crops.name: Chives
crops.notes: Hardy perennial; divide clumps every few years.

crops.name: Mint
crops.notes: Spreads aggressively — grow in a pot or sunken container.

crops.name: Oregano
crops.notes: Drought tolerant once established; flavor best before flowering.

crops.name: Thyme
crops.notes: Needs sharp drainage; avoid wet winter soil.

crops.name: Rosemary
crops.notes: Not winter-hardy below zone 7 — bring pots indoors.

crops.name: Field corn (dent)
crops.notes: Starchy corn for cornmeal, grits and animal feed. Sow 1–2 in deep when soil is 50–60°F+, rows 30 in apart, in a block. Let ears dry on the stalk (husks brown, a black layer at the kernel tip) and finish drying indoors. Isolate corn types: keep field corn, popcorn, Indian corn and sweet corn ~250–300 ft apart, or plant them so tasseling is at least 14 days apart, so pollen from one does not spoil another.

crops.name: Popcorn
crops.notes: Direct sow when soil is ~60°F, 1–2 in deep, 8 in apart, at least 4 rows 18–30 in apart. Most varieties need 85–120 days. Plant popcorn about 3 weeks before sweet corn so they don’t tassel together. Leave ears on the stalk to dry; store when a test batch pops crisp (13–14% moisture). Isolate corn types: keep field corn, popcorn, Indian corn and sweet corn ~250–300 ft apart, or plant them so tasseling is at least 14 days apart, so pollen from one does not spoil another.

crops.name: Indian corn (flint / ornamental)
crops.notes: Colorful hard (flint) or soft (flour) kernels for fall decoration, cornmeal and hominy. Grow like field corn in blocks; let ears dry fully on the stalk, then pull husks back and hang to finish drying. Isolate corn types: keep field corn, popcorn, Indian corn and sweet corn ~250–300 ft apart, or plant them so tasseling is at least 14 days apart, so pollen from one does not spoil another.

crops.name: Winter wheat
crops.notes: Sow in FALL (after your area’s Hessian-fly-free date — about late Sep to mid Oct in southern Illinois), 1–1.5 in deep in rows ~6 in apart. It sprouts, sits through winter, and heads out in spring. Harvest in early summer when heads are golden and kernels are hard; thresh and winnow.

crops.name: Spring wheat
crops.notes: Sow as early in spring as the soil can be worked (soil ~40°F), 1–1.5 in deep in rows ~6 in apart. Best in northern areas with cool summers; in warm climates grow winter wheat instead.

crops.name: Oats
crops.notes: Plant in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked — yields drop if planting slips past early April in central Illinois. Choose hulless (naked) oats for home kitchen use. Also a good spring cover crop. Winter oats survive only mild winters (roughly south of US-50 in Illinois).

crops.name: Barley
crops.notes: Spring barley: sow in very early spring, 1–1.5 in deep in rows ~6 in apart. Winter barley can be sown in early fall (mid-Sep to early Oct) in zone 6 and warmer. Hulless types are easiest for home use; harvest when heads droop and kernels are hard.

src.t: K-State L818 — Kansas Crop Planting Guide

crops.name: Rye (cereal rye)
crops.notes: The hardiest winter grain and the most popular garden cover crop. Sow in fall (early–mid Oct is typical; it still sprouts in cool soil). For grain, harvest in early summer. As a cover crop, cut or mow it at heading (before seed forms) and let it rest 2–3 weeks before planting — rye residue can hold back small seeds.

src.t: Illinois Agronomy Handbook — Small Grains and Sorghum
K-State L818 — Kansas Crop Planting Guide

crops.name: Sorghum (grain / sweet)
crops.notes: Heat- and drought-tough; does best in southern Illinois and warmer. Wait until soil is 60–65°F (about a month after last frost). Sow 1 in deep, thin to 6–10 in, rows 30 in apart. Even a light frost kills it. Sweet sorghum canes are pressed for syrup.

src.t: Illinois Agronomy Handbook — Small Grains and Sorghum
K-State L818 — Kansas Crop Planting Guide

crops.name: Amaranth (grain)
crops.notes: Sow tiny seeds ¼ in deep about 2 weeks after last frost; thin to 6–10 in. Drought tolerant; avoid heavy nitrogen (plants flop). Seeds ripen unevenly — shake heads into a bag as they ripen or cut heads after the first frost, then thresh and winnow. Young leaves are edible greens.

src.t: OMAFRA Specialty Cropportunities — Grain Amaranth

crops.name: Paste tomato (Roma)
crops.notes: Thick, meaty flesh with few seeds — best for sauce, paste, canning and drying. Most (Roma, Viva Italia) are determinate and ripen over a few weeks; San Marzano and Amish Paste (heirloom) are indeterminate. Prone to blossom-end rot — water evenly and mulch.

support.tip: Many paste tomatoes stay shorter, but some grow tall. A cage or stake still helps keep fruit clean and off the soil.

crops.name: Beefsteak tomato
crops.notes: The largest tomatoes (often 1 lb+), dense flesh with many small seed cavities; usually indeterminate and late (80–90+ days from transplant). Give tall cages or stakes and 2–3 ft spacing. Heirlooms like Brandywine and Cherokee Purple are prized for flavor; hybrids like Big Beef add disease resistance. Uneven watering or cool nights cause cracking and catfacing.

support.tip: These plants get big and heavy. Use a tall, strong cage or a sturdy stake, and tie the stems gently as they grow.

crops.name: Sweet pepper (non-bell)
crops.notes: Long or tapered sweet peppers — Cubanelle, banana, Italian frying (Corno di Toro, Jimmy Nardello), pimento and shishito. Usually earlier and more prolific than bells (about 60–80 days from transplant). Pick green/yellow, or let them ripen red for the sweetest flavor.

crops.name: Red potato (early season)
crops.notes: Early (about 70–85 days after emergence), e.g. Dark Red Norland. Waxy flesh holds its shape — boiling, roasting, potato salad. Dig "new" potatoes about 7–8 weeks after planting. Medium yield, some scab resistance; best eaten within a few months.

src.t: Univ. of Illinois Extension HortAnswers — Potato

crops.name: Yellow potato (Yukon Gold, early–mid)
crops.notes: Yukon Gold is early (about 70–85 days after emergence); Yellow Finn is mid-season (85–100). Buttery yellow flesh for baking, mashing and roasting. Yukon Gold is high-yielding and stores well for an early type.

src.t: Univ. of Illinois Extension HortAnswers — Potato

crops.name: Russet potato (late season)
crops.notes: Late (100+ days after emergence), e.g. Russet Burbank — dry, mealy flesh for baking and fries, and the best keeper. Needs a long season, deep loose soil and steady moisture; stress causes knobby or hollow tubers. (Russet Norkotah and Norgold are earlier russets.) Too big for most containers.

crops.name: Fingerling potato (late season)
crops.notes: Small, finger-shaped, firm and waxy — roast or boil whole. Most fingerlings are late (about 100–135 days). Plant whole small seed tubers rather than cut pieces.

crops.name: Lima bean (butter bean)
crops.notes: Needs warmer soil than snap beans (about 65°F) — sow 2–3 weeks after your last frost. Bush types (Henderson, Fordhook) bear sooner; pole types (Sieva, King of the Garden) climb and keep going. 75–90 days. Shell when pods are plump and bright green.

support.tip: Bush lima beans stay short and do not need a support. Pole types climb, so give those a trellis or a teepee.

crops.name: Dry / shelling bean
crops.notes: Grown like bush beans but left on the plant until pods are dry and rattle (about 85–105 days). Pull plants, finish drying under cover, then thresh. Store dry beans in jars.

src.t: Texas A&M AgriLife (Lubbock Master Gardeners) — Vegetable Planting Calendar, recommended varieties (Hound research)

crops.name: Apple
crops.notes: Plant in full sun and well-drained soil. Plant at least two varieties so they cross-pollinate (Winesap and Turley have sterile pollen, so they can’t be the pollinizer). On dwarfing rootstock keep the graft union 3–4 in above the soil; standard trees go below. Head the new tree back to about 30 in after planting. Dwarf trees may bear at 2–3 years old and may need a support stake.

src.t: Illinois Extension — Apples (Fruit Trees for Home Gardens) (Hound research)
Illinois Extension — Fruitfulness and Pollination
Purdue HO-190 — Fruits and Nuts for Edible Landscaping (years to bearing, Table 1)

crops.pollination: Plant at least two different apple varieties (or a crabapple) within about 300 ft. Winesap and Turley pollen is sterile, so they cannot be the helper tree.
crops.care: Head the new tree back after planting. Dwarf trees need a stake. Do not spray insect killers while trees bloom — bees do the pollinating.

crops.name: Grape
crops.notes: Plant in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, 8 ft apart in the row and 10 ft between rows. Build a sturdy trellis before the second season (four-cane Kniffin: wires about 3 ft and 5½–6 ft high). Expect fruit from about the third year; a planting can stay productive 20–30 years. Grapes are very sensitive to 2,4-D weed-killer drift — keep lawn herbicides away.

src.t: Illinois Extension — Planting and Care of Backyard Grapes (Hound research)
MU Extension G6085 — Home Fruit Production: Grape Culture (Hound research)

support.tip: Grapes need a strong, lasting trellis or arbor. Put the support in place before the vines get heavy, and tie new canes gently as they grow.

crops.name: Pecan
crops.notes: A big, long-lived nut tree — years before a real crop. In the Midwest choose cold-hardy “northern” cultivars. Pecans have separate male and female flowers that open at different times (Type I and Type II), so plant both types for good pollination. Pecan scab is the most damaging disease; pick resistant cultivars.

src.t: MU Center for Agroforestry AF1002 — Growing Pecans in Missouri (2022) (Hound research)

crops.name: Black walnut
crops.notes: A native tree (70–90 ft) that is hard to transplant, so it is grown from nuts planted in fall in deep, rich, well-drained soil. ⚠️ Its roots, buds and nut hulls release juglone, which yellows, wilts and can kill sensitive garden plants such as tomatoes — keep vegetable beds well away from black walnut trees and don’t compost the hulls for the garden.

src.t: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Black Walnut, Juglans nigra (Hound research)

crops.name: Orange (sweet orange)
crops.notes: Subtropical — not hardy where it freezes. In zone 7 grow a dwarf tree (grafted on a dwarfing rootstock such as Flying Dragon) in a large pot and bring it indoors before frost. Re-pot or refresh the mix as it grows.

src.t: UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions — Citrus (Hound research)

crops.name: Key lime
crops.notes: Very cold-sensitive: leaves are damaged at 30–32°F and wood is damaged or killed below 29°F. Outside the far south, keep it in a pot in full sun and bring it in well before frost. Tarter, smaller and rounder than the grocery-store Persian (Tahiti) lime.

src.t: UF/IFAS — Key Lime Growing in the Florida Home Landscape (Hound research)
UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions — Citrus (Hound research)

crops.name: Banana (dwarf)
crops.notes: Frost keeps bananas in the tropics and warm subtropics. Plant in full sun. A flower stalk appears 10–15 months after planting and fruit follows; from a small sucker, harvest can take 9–20 months. In zone 7 grow a dwarf type (such as Dwarf Cavendish) in a big pot and bring it indoors for winter.

src.t: UF/IFAS — Banana Growing in the Florida Home Landscape (Hound research)
UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions — Dwarf Fruit Trees (Hound research)

crops.name: Bay laurel (bay leaf)
crops.notes: An evergreen shrub that can reach 12 ft but grows slowly. Pick the leathery leaves and dry them for cooking. North of zone 8 keep it in a pot and overwinter it indoors; new plants are easiest from layering or cuttings.

src.t: UF/IFAS Gardening Solutions — Bay Laurel (Hound research)
MU Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home (Hound research)

crops.name: Fennel (Florence & herb)
crops.notes: Sow directly — the taproot doesn’t transplant well. Herb fennel goes in after the last frost; Florence (bulb) fennel is best sown mid-June to July so the bulb forms in the cooler, shorter days of late summer and fall. Keep the soil evenly moist or it bolts. Hill soil around egg-size bulbs and harvest at tennis-ball size. For seed, cut brown flower heads into a paper bag to dry.

src.t: Illinois Extension — Fennel (Herbs) (Hound research)
MU Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home (Hound research)

crops.name: Lovage
crops.notes: A big, hardy perennial (4–6 ft) with a strong celery flavor. Leaves, stems, roots and seeds are all edible — use the seeds like celery seed. Pick young leaves; dry seed heads in paper bags when they turn brown. Good at the back of a border.

src.t: Illinois Extension — Lovage (Herbs) (Hound research)
MU Extension G6470 — Growing Herbs at Home (Hound research)

crops.name: Ginger
crops.notes: Tropical (zones 8–10) — in colder areas grow it in a pot at least 12 in wide. Plant 2–3 in pieces with 2–3 buds, eyes up, about 2 in deep; keep the mix warm (70–80°F) and barely moist — sprouts take 3–8 weeks. Move outside only when days are 68°F+ and nights stay above 50°F, and bring it in before nights drop below 50°F. Harvest when the leaves yellow and dry, about 8–10 months after planting.

src.t: UVM Extension — Growing Ginger and Turmeric Indoors (Hound research)
UF/IFAS EP638 — Ginger, Galangal, and Turmeric Production in Florida (Hound research)

crops.name: Turmeric
crops.notes: Grown just like ginger: a pot at least 12 in wide, rhizome pieces with 2–3 buds about 2 in deep, warm and barely moist until it sprouts (turmeric is slower than ginger). Plants reach 3–4 ft. Keep above 50°F and harvest when the foliage fades, about 8–10 months after planting. Save a piece to replant.

crops.name: Staghorn sumac
crops.notes: A native shrub to small tree whose fuzzy red fruit clusters ripen in late summer to early autumn and are used for a tangy, lemony spice. Fruit forms on plants 3–4 years old, and most plants are male or female, so you need both. It spreads by root sprouts — 3 ft or more a year — so give it room. ⚠️ Only pick the upright, fuzzy RED clusters; poison sumac has drooping white berries.

crops.name: Sunflower (seed)
crops.notes: Needs full sun. Sow 1–2 in deep after frost; thin tall seed types to 2–2½ ft and stake them in windy spots. Seeds mature 70–100 days after planting — harvest when the head turns down, the back is lemon-yellow and the seeds are plump, then hang heads to dry in paper bags or cheesecloth (birds love them).

crops.name: Sesame
crops.notes: Sow ½ in deep in full sun once the soil is about 70°F (around mid-May), and no later than early July. Keep the seed moist for its first 3 days. About 100 days to full seed maturity plus 1–2 weeks to dry down. Pods burst when ripe (“shatter”), so cut stems as the lower pods turn and finish drying them over a sheet. Benne is the heirloom type.

crops.name: Peanut
crops.notes: Needs loose, sandy soil and at least 120 frost-free days. Plant seeds 1–1½ in deep, 10–12 in apart, rows 36 in apart, in warm soil. Keep the soil loose and hilled — the flower “pegs” must push into it to form nuts. Dig when the leaves turn yellow, usually 110 days or more after planting, shake off dry soil, cure in a warm, dry shed about a week, then air-dry another 1–2 weeks.

crops.name: Rice (bucket rice)
crops.method: Direct sow in a pot standing in water
crops.notes: A fun container crop: fill a 1-gallon pot with soil to 2 in below the rim, sow about 6 seeds ½ in deep and set the pot in a saucer of water in full sun. Seedlings appear in about 10 days — keep the 3 best. Keep the soil wet and feed if leaves yellow. About 120 days from planting to seed; harvest when the grain turns yellow and hard.

crops.name: Chickpea (garbanzo)
crops.notes: A cool-season pulse sown in spring once the soil is about 45°F. Plants take 84–125 days to mature and dry on the plant. Use a chickpea inoculant — the bacteria for peas and lentils don’t work on chickpeas. Kabuli types have large, light seeds; desi types are smaller and darker.

crops.name: Pear
crops.pollination: Plant two or more different varieties for cross-pollination. Some pairs do not work: Maxine and Starking Delicious do not pollinate each other.
crops.care: Feed lightly. Too much new growth makes fire blight (a bacterial disease) worse. Prune less than other fruit trees. Pick pears when mature; they finish ripening in storage.
crops.notes: Grow in full sun and well-drained soil. Fire blight is the main problem. Semi-dwarf trees about 15 ft apart.

crops.name: Peach
crops.pollination: Most peaches are self-fruitful: one tree can make fruit by itself.
crops.care: Many peaches are not winter hardy in cold areas (Reliance is a hardier choice). Prune hard every year and keep the middle open, because fruit grows on last year's shoots. Watch for brown rot, leaf curl and bacterial spot.
crops.notes: Full sun, well-drained soil. About 15 ft apart. Train to an open center (vase shape).

crops.care: Prune every year, but lighter than other fruit trees. Pick ripe cherries quickly. Birds love them.

crops.notes: A fast cool-season green. Sow ⅓–½ inch deep about 3 weeks before the last frost, again 3 weeks later, and again from midsummer for fall. Thin to 3–5 inches (eat the thinnings). Pick leaves young; heat makes them tough and bitter and the plants bolt. Seed mustards (yellow, brown) take 80–95 days to ripen seed.

crops.name: Lentil
crops.notes: A cool-season pulse. Seedlings take frost, so sow a week or two before the last frost once the soil is 40°F: 1 inch deep, 2 inches apart, then thin to 4–6 inches. Too much water can kill them; stop watering when pods start to dry. Dry lentils are ready in about 80–100 days. Green pods can be shelled and eaten like peas.

crops.name: Almond

crops.care: Blooms very early, so spring frost often kills the flowers. In southern Illinois and Missouri the tree may live but rarely makes nuts. Needs about 400–500 chill hours, deep well-drained soil and full sun.
crops.notes: About 15–20 ft apart. Harvest when the hulls split open. Hull and dry the nuts, then freeze them 48 hours before storing.

groups.note: Sweet, field (dent), pop and Indian (flint/flour) corn are all one species and cross-pollinate by wind. Grow just one type, or keep types ~250–300 ft apart, or time plantings so they tassel at least 14 days apart.

groups.name: Tomatoes
groups.note: Types by fruit: standard/slicing, beefsteak (largest, latest), salad (cherry, grape) and paste (Roma). Determinate (bush) plants ripen their crop over 4–6 weeks — handy for canning; indeterminate (vining) plants bear until frost and need tall stakes or cages. Heirloom = an open-pollinated variety (usually pre-1940) whose saved seed comes true; often great flavor and color, but usually later, less productive and less disease resistant than hybrids. Any type can be heirloom or hybrid.

groups.name: Potatoes
groups.note: Grouped by days to maturity after the sprouts come up: early (about 70–85 days), mid-season (85–100) and late (100+). Early types give "new" potatoes by early summer; late types yield and store best. Plant certified seed potatoes 2–4 weeks before your last frost once soil is 45°F+. Grocery potatoes are often treated to stop sprouting — fine for a fun kitchen-scrap experiment, but certified seed is disease-free and more reliable.

groups.note: Summer squash is picked young and tender all summer; winter squash and pumpkins ripen a hard rind for storage. Squash cross-pollinate within a species — it does not change this year’s fruit, only saved seed.

groups.name: Melons
groups.note: Melons need heat, full sun and steady water until fruit sizes up; ease off watering as they ripen for sweeter fruit. Use black plastic or transplants in shorter seasons.

groups.name: Cabbage family (cole crops)
groups.note: Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale and Brussels sprouts are all the same species. They like cool weather, share the same pests (cabbage worms, flea beetles) and should be rotated together.

src.t: Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331 — Vegetable Planting Guide (Hound research)

groups.name: Onion family
groups.note: Onions, garlic, leeks and chives share pests and diseases (onion thrips, onion maggot) — rotate them together.

src.t: Virginia Cooperative Extension 426-331 — Vegetable Planting Guide (Hound research)

groups.name: Citrus
groups.note: Citrus is subtropical: lemons and limes (the “acid” citrus) are the most cold-sensitive, sweet oranges a little less so, and the Meyer lemon is the most cold-tolerant. Outside zones 9–11, grow dwarf trees (on a dwarfing rootstock such as Flying Dragon) in large pots and bring them indoors before frost.
